items.headline: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding. Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language.
items.summary: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly.
items.headline_tr: VFlash: Flash Primitive Decoding ile Hızlı, Doğru Görsel Planlama. Robotik ve otonom sürüş gibi fiziksel yapay zeka görevlerine yönelik modellerin yalnızca dilde akıl yürütmesi gerekmez.
items.summary_tr: Robotik ve otonom sürüş gibi fiziksel yapay zeka görevlerine yönelik modellerin yalnızca dilde akıl yürütmesi gerekmez. Uzamsal hedefleri temsil etmek ve hareketi tahmin etmek için görsel planları (noktalar, sınırlayıcı kutular ve yörüngeler) kullanabilirler. Bununla birlikte, otoregresif vizyon dili modelleri bu planları her seferinde bir koordinat jetonu oluşturarak daha zengin tahminlerin artmasını sağlar.

detail.problem_context: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language.
detail.method_architecture: They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

detail.findings_tradeoffs_tr: Flash Primitive Decoding yoluyla hızlı, doğru görsel planlamaya yönelik bir yöntem olan VFlash'ı tanıtıyoruz. VFlash, koordinatlarını ortaklaşa tahmin etmek için görsel temel öğelerin bilinen yapısından yararlanır.

items.headline: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training
items.summary: Harness evolution from a common base exhibits Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity: variants repair different failures, and their utility changes as the policy learns. Rather than seeking a universally superior harness, we introduce Harness-S to selectively rescue failures of a base execution system through sibling harnesses and transfer the resulting capabilities into a single policy that remains effective under the original harness. Directional Harness Evolution develops specialized sibling harnesses along distinct repair directions, forming a reusable Sibling Harness Pool that remains fixed during policy training.

items.headline: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand
items.summary: Benchmark compression reduces the often prohibitive time and cost of model evaluation by evaluating models on a small benchmark subset that closely matches full-benchmark results. To quantify estimation error, we derive an accurate analytical approximation to the error distribution when estimating full-benchmark scores from a subset, showing that most subsets yield small errors, while a few produce much larger errors, resulting in a long-tailed distribution. This means random sampling alone can achieve surprisingly strong performance with high probability, but remains unstable due to rare large errors.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: We further show that this instability is inherent to modern foundation models and persists even as more models are evaluated. Based on these findings, we introduce BestRand, a stable and low-cost benchmark compression method that preserves the efficiency of random sampling while substantially reducing its high-error tail. We validate BestRand on 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, and further extend it to VLA evaluation. Compared with competitive methods, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4% on average, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost. It further reduces OOD estimation error by 21.8% on average across score-range, model-family, and temporal shifts. Together, our theory provides practical guidance for understanding and predicting the accuracy and reliability of benchmark compression, while BestRand enables stable and accurate compression at low cost. items.headline: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing
items.summary: Strong single-turn editing performance does not guarantee reliable multi-turn interaction: as edited outputs are repeatedly reused, small unintended changes can accumulate into severe visual drift. This long-term drift is often mitigated through training on multi-turn data or cross-turn rollouts, potentially altering pretrained priors, or through specialized inference-time mechanisms that are difficult to scale to foundation models. We introduce TailSteer, a final-stage training framework that improves multi-turn robustness while retaining the generative and editing capabilities acquired through earlier training.

items.headline: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents
items.summary: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence.

detail.method_architecture: We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either model's neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share an evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by a decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. A single frozen LimiX-2 predictor serves all five task categories. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. On ToolPRMBench's BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, absolute accuracy gains are 34.26% and 28.87%, respectively, at the methods' respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy improves as history grows. With identical imbalanced histories, mean balanced accuracy improves by an absolute 14.51% across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability, creating a shared route for advances in conditional prediction to improve decisions across agent tasks.

items.headline: D3D: Decoupled Diffusion Drafting for Asynchronous Speculative Decoding
items.summary: Target-conditioned diffusion drafters predict candidate tokens in parallel, yet each new block must wait for updated target-model hidden states. This forces drafting and verification to run sequentially, limiting speedup even though each block is generated in one pass. We introduce D3D, a standalone diffusion drafter that removes this inter-round dependency.
items.headline_tr: D3D: Eşzamansız Spekülatif Kod Çözme için Ayrıştırılmış Yayılım Taslağı
items.summary_tr: Hedef koşullu yayılma taslağı hazırlayıcıları aday tokenleri paralel olarak tahmin eder, ancak her yeni bloğun güncellenmiş hedef model gizli durumlarını beklemesi gerekir. Bu, taslak hazırlama ve doğrulamanın sıralı olarak çalışmasını zorlayarak, her bloğun tek geçişte oluşturulmasına rağmen hızlanmayı sınırlandırır. Bu turlar arası bağımlılığı ortadan kaldıran bağımsız bir difüzyon hazırlayıcı olan D3D'yi tanıtıyoruz.

items.headline: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents
items.summary: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: In this paper, we introduce EvoMemState, a state-centric framework that augments persistent facts with two complementary states: Relational States that capture how facts remain valid and relate to one another as memory evolves, and a Reasoning State that determines how these facts should be applied to the current request. Specifically, EvoMemState consists of three key components: (i) Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts and constructs Relational States that maintain their validity, scope, and evolving relations. (ii) RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memory-use experience into a policy through reinforcement learning to generate a request-specific Reasoning State. (iii) State-Aware Reasoning then combines the relevant facts with their Relational States and the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agent. Extensive experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/EvoMemState.git.

items.summary: Multimodal agents use web and image tools to answer questions beyond their internal knowledge. items.summary_tr: Multimodal temsilciler, dahili bilgilerinin ötesindeki soruları yanıtlamak için web ve görsel araçlarını kullanır. detail.findings_tradeoffs: We therefore focus on visual context management. This involves organizing and using visual information and linking it to other findings during search. Visually intensive tasks require agents to combine object appearance, local details, or spatial relations with external information. We introduce VisSearch-Bench, with 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. It covers Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide-Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task provides a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete task success, while Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, even with search tools. These results highlight the challenge of linking visual evidence with search results to produce complete answers.

items.headline: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex
items.summary: Autoregressive approaches with large language models, such as long chain-of-thought reasoning, have become the default for new AI applications because they reach higher accuracy on a wide range of tasks. In production, however, they give inconsistent answers, require parsing of outputs, and add cost and latency. Decision models address this: given a question and a set of options supplied by the user, they return a probability distribution over the options without autoregressive decoding.

detail.method_architecture: In production, however, they give inconsistent answers, require parsing of outputs, and add cost and latency. Decision models address this: given a question and a set of options supplied by the user, they return a probability distribution over the options without autoregressive decoding.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: We present Drex, a family of four open decision models with 8B (DLM), 9B (v1.5), 35B with 3B active (v2.0), and 27B (Max) parameters. Each request consists of a state (a document, record, or agent context, optionally with images) and questions about it, each asking for a choice among options, a yes/no judgment, or a score on an ordered scale. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), plus vision tuning for Max. Ablations show that RLAF improves accuracy and that consistency losses improve robustness to option order. On Decision Index 0.4.1, Max sets a new state of the art among the decision models we compare (67.52 on the public suite vs. 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0). On Decision Bench v4, it is statistically tied with d3-turbo and GPT-6 Sol and trails Claude Opus 5.5 by 1.6 points, and it has the highest accuracy among decision models on DecideBench. Max answers a typical request in 183 ms, against about 2.0 s for GPT-6 Sol and 3.5 s for Claude Opus 5.5, and its outputs are stable under option reordering. All four models are open source: https://github.com/nace-ai/drex-decision-models

items.headline: Doom GPU Flame Graphs
items.summary: Imagine halving the resource costs of AI and what that could mean for the planet and the industry -- based on extreme estimates such savings could reduce the total US power usage by over 10% by 2030 1 . At Intel we've been creating a new analyzer tool to help reduce AI costs called AI Flame Graphs : a visualization that shows an AI accelerator or GPU hardware profile along with the full software stack, based on my CPU flame graphs . Our first version is available to customers in the Intel Tiber AI Cloud as a preview for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series (previously called Ponte Vecchio).

detail.problem_context: Imagine halving the resource costs of AI and what that could mean for the planet and the industry -- based on extreme estimates such savings could reduce the total US power usage by over 10% by 2030 1 .
detail.method_architecture: At Intel we've been creating a new analyzer tool to help reduce AI costs called AI Flame Graphs : a visualization that shows an AI accelerator or GPU hardware profile along with the full software stack, based on my CPU flame graphs . Our first version is available to customers in the Intel Tiber AI Cloud as a preview for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series (previously called Ponte Vecchio).
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Here is an example: Simple example: SYCL matrix multiply microbenchmark (Click for interactive SVG .) The green frames are the actual instructions running on the AI or GPU accelerator, aqua shows the source code for these functions, and red (C), yellow (C++), and orange (kernel) show the CPU code paths that initiated these AI/GPU programs. The gray "-" frames just help highlight the boundary between CPU and AI/GPU code. The x-axis is proportional to cost, so you look for the widest things and find ways to reduce them. Layers This flame graph shows a simple program for SYCL (a high-level C++ language for accelerators) that tests three implementations of matrix multiply, running them with the same input workload. The flame graph is dominated by the slowest implementation, multiply_basic(), which doesn't use any optimizations and consumes at 72% of stall samples and is shown as the widest tower. On the right are two thin towers for multiply_local_access() at 21% which replaces the accessor with a local variable, and multiply_local_access_and_tiling() at 6% which also adds matrix tiling. The towers are getting smaller as optimizations are added. This flame graph profiler is a prototype based on Intel EU stall profiling for hardware profiling and eBPF for software instrumentation. It's designed to be easy and low-overhead , just like a CPU profiler. You should be able to generate a flame graph of an existing AI workload whenever you want, without having to restart anything or launch additional code via an interposer. Instruction-offset Profiling This is not the first project to build an AI profiler or even something called an AI Flame Graph, however, others I've seen focus on tracing CPU stacks and timing accelerator execution, but don't profile the instruction offsets running on the accelerator; or do profile them but via expensive binary instrumentation. I wanted to build AI flame graphs that work like CPU flame graphs: Easy to use, negligible cost, production safe, and shows everything. A daily tool for developers, with most of the visualization in the language of the developer : source code functions. This has been an internal AI project at Intel for the past year. Intel was already investing in this space, building the EU stall profiler capability for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series that provides an approximation of HW instruction sampling. I was lucky to have Dr. Matthew (Ben) Olson , an Intel AI engineer who has also worked on eBPF performance tooling ( processwatch ) as well as memory management research, join my team and do most of the development work. His background has helped us power through difficulties that seemed insurmountable. We've also recently been joined by Dr. Brandon Kammerdiener (coincidentally another graduate of the University of Tennessee, like Ben), who also has eBPF and memory internals experience, and has been helping us take on harder and harder workloads. And Gabriel Muñoz just joined today to help with releases. Now that our small team has shown that this is possible, we'll be joined by other teams at Intel to develop this further. We could have built a harder-to-use and higher-overhead version months ago using Intel GTPin but for widespread adoption it needs minimal overhead and ease of use so that developers don't hesitate to use this daily and to add it to deployment pipelines. What's a Flame Graph? A flame graph is a visualization I invented in 2011 for showing sampled code stack traces. It has become the standard for CPU profiling and analysis, helping developers quickly find performance improvements and eliminate regressions. A CPU flame graph shows the "big picture" of running software, with x-axis proportional to CPU cost. The example picture on the right summarizes how easy it can be to go from compute costs to responsible code paths. Prior to flame graphs, it could take hours to understand a complex profile by reading through hundreds of pages of output . Now it takes seconds: all you have to do is look for the widest rectangles. Flame graphs have had worldwide adoption. They have been the basis for five startups so far, have been adopted in over thirty performance analysis products, and have had over eighty implementations . My first implementation of flame graphs took a few hours on a Wednesday night after work. The real effort has been in the decade since, where I worked with different profilers, runtimes, libraries, kernels, compilers, and hypervisors to get flame graphs working properly in different environments, including fixing stack walking and symbolization. Earlier this year I posted about the final missing piece: Helping distros enable frame pointers so that profiling works across standard system libraries. Similar work is necessary for AI workloads: fixing stacks and symbols and getting profiling to work for different hardware, kernel drivers, user-mode drivers, frameworks, runtimes, languages, and models. A lot more work, too, as AI analysis has less maturity than CPU analysis. Searching Samples If you are new to flame graphs, it's worth mentioning the built-in search capability. In the earlier example, most of the stall samples are caused by sbid: software scoreboard dependency. As that may be a unique search term, you can run search (Ctrl-F, or click "Search") on "sbid" and it will highlight it in magenta: Search also shows the total number of stack samples that contained sbid in the bottom right: 78.4%. You can search for any term in the flame graph: accelerator instructions, source paths, function names, etc., to quickly calculate the percentage of stacks where it is present (excluding vertical overlap) helping you prioritise performance work. Note that the samples are EU stall-based, which means theoretical performance wins can take the percentages down to zero. This is different to timer-based samples as are typically used in CPU profiling. Stalls mean you better focus on the pain, the parts of the code that aren't making forward progress, but you aren't seeing resource usage by unstalled instructions. I'd like to supuport timer-based samples in the future as well, so we can have both views. Who will use this? At a recent golang conference, I asked the audience of 200+ to raise their hands if they were using CPU flame graphs. Almost every hand went up. I know of companies where flame graphs are a daily tool that developers use to understand and tune their code, reducing compute costs. This will become a daily tool for AI developers. My employer will use this as well for evaluation analysis, to find areas to tune to beat competitors, as well as to better understand workload performance to aid design. Why is AI profiling hard? Consider CPU instruction profiling: This is easy when the program and symbol table are both in the file system and in a standardized file format (such as ELF) as is the case with native compiled code (C). CPU profiling gets hard for JIT-complied code, like Java, as instructions and symbols are dynamically generated and placed in main memory (the process heap) without following a universal standard. For such JITted code we use runtime-specific methods and agents to retrieve snapshots of the heap information, which is different for each runtime. AI workloads also have different runtimes (and frameworks, languages, user-mode drivers, compilers, etc.) any of which can require special tinkering to get their CPU stacks and symbols to work. These CPU stacks are shown as the red, orange, and yellow frames in the AI Flame Graph. Some AI workloads are easy to get these frames working, some (like PyTorch) are a lot more work. But the real challenge is instruction profiling of actual GPU and AI accelerator programs -- shown as the aqua and green frames -- and correctly associating them with the CPU stacks beneath them. Not only may these GPU and AI programs not exist in the file system, but they may not even exist in main memory! Even for running programs. Once execution begins, they may be deallocated from main memory and only exist in special accelerator memory, beyond the direct reach of OS profilers and debuggers. Or within reach, but only through a prohibitively high-overhead HW-specific debugger interface. There's also no /proc representation for these programs either (I've been proposing building an equivalent) so there's no direct way to even tell what is running and what isn't, and all the other /proc details. Forget instruction profiling, even ps(1) and all the other process tools do not work. It's been a mind-bending experience, revealing what gets taken for granted because it has existed in CPU land for decades: A process table. Process tools. Standard file formats. Programs that exist in the file system. Programs running from main memory. Debuggers. Profiliers. Core dumping. Disassembling. Single stepping. Static and dynamic instrumentation. Etc. For GPUs and AI, this is all far less mature. It can make the work exciting at times, when you think something is impossible and then find or devise a way. Fortunately we have a head start as some things do exist. Depending on the runtime and kernel driver, there are debug interfaces where you can list running accelerator programs and other statistics, as used by tools like intel_gpu_top(1). You can kill -9 a GPU workload using intel_gpu_abrt(1). Some interfaces can even generate basic ELF files for the running accelerator programs that you can try to load in a debugger like gdb(1). And there is support for GPU/AI program disassembly, if you can get your hands on the binary. It feels to me like GPU/AI debugging, OS style, is about two years old. Better than zero, but still early on, and lots more ahead of us. A decade, at least. What do AI developers think of this? We've shown AI Flame Graphs to other AI developers at Intel and a common reaction is to be a bit puzzled, wondering what to do with it. AI developers think about their bit of code, but with AI Flame Graphs they can now see the entire stack for the first time, including the HW, and many layers they don't usually think about or don't know about. It basically looks like a pile of gibberish with their code only a small part of the flame graph. CPU Flame Graph Implementations This reaction is similar to people's first experiences with CPU flame graphs, which show parts of the system that developers and engineers typically don't work on, such as runtime internals, system libraries, and kernel internals. Flame graphs are great at highlighting the dozen or so functions that matter the most, so it becomes a problem of learning what those functions do across a few different code bases, which are typically open source. Understanding a dozen such functions can take a few hours or even a few days -- but if this leads to a 10% or 2x cost win, it is time well spent. And the next time the user looks at a flame graph, they start saying "I've seen that function before" and so on. You can get to the point where understanding the bulk of a CPU flame graph takes less than a minute: look for the widest tower, click to zoom, read the frames, done. I'm encouraged by the success of CPU flame graphs, with over 80 implementations and countless real world case studies. Sometimes I'm browsing a performance issue I care about on github and hit page down and there's a CPU flame graph. They are everywhere. I expect AI developers will also be able to understand AI Flame Graphs in less than a minute, but to start with people will be spending a day or more browsing code bases they didn't know were involved. Publishing case studies of found wins will also help people learn how to interpret them, and also help explain the value. What about PyTorch? Another common reaction we've had is that AI developers are using PyTorch, and initially we didn't support it as it meant walking Python stacks, which isn't trivial. detail.abstract_excerpt: Imagine halving the resource costs of AI and what that could mean for the planet and the industry -- based on extreme estimates such savings could reduce the total US power usage by over 10% by 2030 1 . At Intel we've been creating a new analyzer tool to help reduce AI costs called AI Flame Graphs : a visualization that shows an AI accelerator or GPU hardware profile along with the full software stack, based on my CPU flame graphs . Our first version is available to customers in the Intel Tiber AI Cloud as a preview for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series (previously called Ponte Vecchio). Here is an example: Simple example: SYCL matrix multiply microbenchmark (Click for interactive SVG .) The green frames are the actual instructions running on the AI or GPU accelerator, aqua shows the source code for these functions, and red (C), yellow (C++), and orange (kernel) show the CPU code paths that initiated these AI/GPU programs. The gray "-" frames just help highlight the boundary between CPU and AI/GPU code. The x-axis is proportional to cost, so you look for the widest things and find ways to reduce them. Layers This flame graph shows a simple program for SYCL (a high-level C++ language for accelerators) that tests three implementations of matrix multiply, running them with the same input workload. The flame graph is dominated by the slowest implementation, multiply_basic(), which doesn't use any optimizations and consumes at 72% of stall samples and is shown as the widest tower. On the right are two thin towers for multiply_local_access() at 21% which replaces the accessor with a local variable, and multiply_local_access_and_tiling() at 6% which also adds matrix tiling. The towers are getting smaller as optimizations are added. This flame graph profiler is a prototype based on Intel EU stall profiling for hardware profiling and eBPF for software instrumentation. It's designed to be easy and low-overhead , just like a CPU profiler. You should be able to generate a flame graph of an existing AI workload whenever you want, without having to restart anything or launch additional code via an interposer. Instruction-offset Profiling This is not the first project to build an AI profiler or even something called an AI Flame Graph, however, others I've seen focus on tracing CPU stacks and timing accelerator execution, but don't profile the instruction offsets running on the accelerator; or do profile them but via expensive binary instrumentation. I wanted to build AI flame graphs that work like CPU flame graphs: Easy to use, negligible cost, production safe, and shows everything. A daily tool for developers, with most of the visualization in the language of the developer : source code functions. This has been an internal AI project at Intel for the past year. Intel was already investing in this space, building the EU stall profiler capability for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series that provides an approximation of HW instruction sampling. I was lucky to have Dr. Matthew (Ben) Olson , an Intel AI engineer who has also worked on eBPF performance tooling ( processwatch ) as well as memory management research, join my team and do most of the development work. His background has helped us power through difficulties that seemed insurmountable. We've also recently been joined by Dr. Brandon Kammerdiener (coincidentally another graduate of the University of Tennessee, like Ben), who also has eBPF and memory internals experience, and has been helping us take on harder and harder workloads. And Gabriel Muñoz just joined today to help with releases. Now that our small team has shown that this is possible, we'll be joined by other teams at Intel to develop this further. We could have built a harder-to-use and higher-overhead version months ago using Intel GTPin but for widespread adoption it needs minimal overhead and ease of use so that developers don't hesitate to use this daily and to add it to deployment pipelines. What's a Flame Graph? A flame graph is a visualization I invented in 2011 for showing sampled code stack traces. It has become the standard for CPU profiling and analysis, helping developers quickly find performance improvements and eliminate regressions. A CPU flame graph shows the "big picture" of running software, with x-axis proportional to CPU cost. The example picture on the right summarizes how easy it can be to go from compute costs to responsible code paths. Prior to flame graphs, it could take hours to understand a complex profile by reading through hundreds of pages of output . Now it takes seconds: all you have to do is look for the widest rectangles. Flame graphs have had worldwide adoption. They have been the basis for five startups so far, have been adopted in over thirty performance analysis products, and have had over eighty implementations . My first implementation of flame graphs took a few hours on a Wednesday night after work. The real effort has been in the decade since, where I worked with different profilers, runtimes, libraries, kernels, compilers, and hypervisors to get flame graphs working properly in different environments, including fixing stack walking and symbolization. Earlier this year I posted about the final missing piece: Helping distros enable frame pointers so that profiling works across standard system libraries. Similar work is necessary for AI workloads: fixing stacks and symbols and getting profiling to work for different hardware, kernel drivers, user-mode drivers, frameworks, runtimes, languages, and models. A lot more work, too, as AI analysis has less maturity than CPU analysis. Searching Samples If you are new to flame graphs, it's worth mentioning the built-in search capability. In the earlier example, most of the stall samples are caused by sbid: software scoreboard dependency. As that may be a unique search term, you can run search (Ctrl-F, or click "Search") on "sbid" and it will highlight it in magenta: Search also shows the total number of stack samples that contained sbid in the bottom right: 78.4%. items.headline: Averages of sub-additive functions through non-Følner sequences
items.summary: We study the quantity $\sup_{φ\inΦ}\limsup_{n\to\infty}φ(F_n)/|F_n|$, where $\mathcal F= (F_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence of finite subsets of a countable amenable group, and $Φ$ is a collection of subadditive functions. Under mild conditions on $Φ$ we prove that the aforementioned quantity equals the supremum over $φ\inΦ$ of the limit of $φ(F)/|F|$ as $F$ becomes more and more invariant, multiplied by a ``Følnerness'' constant $C(\mathcal F)\in[1,\infty]$. We have $C(\mathcal F)=1$ if and only if $\mathcal F$ is Følner.

items.summary: Convex cooperative games have a nonempty core and admit an efficient construction of core allocations. However, economically natural local frictions may violate convexity. items.headline: Transparency in Team Contracts. In contract design, the principal is often better informed about the project's chances of succeeding than the agents.
items.summary: In contract design, the principal is often better informed about the project's chances of succeeding than the agents. To incentivize effort, the principal has two main tools: first, to design a contract, sharing part of the project's success among the agents; second, to design a (Bayesian) persuasion scheme, selectively sharing information with the agents. In this work we are interested in the optimal combination of both these tools.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: We tackle the joint problem through the prism of simplicity vs. optimality, and establish a stark dichotomy: The simple disclosure scheme of full transparency achieves a tight $4/3$-approximation to the optimal combination of information disclosure and team contract, when the team's production function is submodular. items.headline: Polynomial-Time Computation of Extensive-Form Proper Equilibria in Two-Player Zero-Sum Games
items.summary: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for computing an exact extensive-form proper equilibrium in a finite two-player zero-sum extensive-form game with perfect recall and rational data. Properness is understood in the agent normal form: an action at an information set is penalized relative to a better action while all other local behavioral choices, including the player's own future actions, remain fixed. Our algorithm assigns each information set a geometric permutahedron of allowable action probabilities.

items.headline: Stability and Perfection in Constrained Weighted Network Games
items.summary: We introduce a general framework of constrained weighted network formation in which agents allocate resources across coalitional interactions while facing feasibility constraints. More precisely, we allow arbitrary coalitions of agents to be assigned a continuous weight, and we incorporate both coalitional capacity constraints and individual budget constraints into the model. This framework extends the weighted network formation model of Bich and Morhaim by combining continuous interaction intensities with endogenous feasibility restrictions.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Within this setting, we introduce a new notion of stability -- called coalitionwise stability -- extending pairwise stability to constrained network games. Under standard continuity and componentwise quasiconcavity assumptions on payoff functions, we establish the existence of coalitionwise stable networks. We then investigate refinements of stability inspired by the notion of perfect equilibrium introduced by Selten, and by the notion of perfect pairwise stability developed by Bich and Teteryatnikova for network games. The presence of feasibility constraints fundamentally alters the geometry of the feasible set, which no longer possesses a product structure. As a consequence, trembling-hand type refinements become substantially more delicate, since perturbations of some interactions may render other interactions infeasible. In particular, we show the equivalence between these trembling-hand and perturbative formulations under some componentwise monotonicity assumption.

items.headline: Bypassing Administrator Protection by Abusing UI Access. A headline feature introduced in the latest release of Windows 11, 25H2 is Administrator Protection.
items.summary: A headline feature introduced in the latest release of Windows 11, 25H2 is Administrator Protection. The goal of this feature is to replace User Account Control (UAC) with a more robust and importantly, securable system to allow a local user to access administrator privileges only when necessary. This blog post will give a brief overview of the new feature, how it works and how it’s different from UAC.

detail.abstract_excerpt: A headline feature introduced in the latest release of Windows 11, 25H2 is Administrator Protection. The goal of this feature is to replace User Account Control (UAC) with a more robust and importantly, securable system to allow a local user to access administrator privileges only when necessary. This blog post will give a brief overview of the new feature, how it works and how it’s different from UAC. I’ll then describe some of the security research I undertook while it was in the insider preview builds on Windows 11. Finally I’ll detail one of the nine separate vulnerabilities that I found to bypass the feature to silently gain full administrator privileges. All the issues that I reported to Microsoft have been fixed, either prior to the feature being officially released (in optional update KB5067036) or as subsequent security bulletins. Note: As of 1st December 2025 the Administrator Protection feature has been disabled by Microsoft while an application compatibility issue is dealt with. The issue is unlikely to be related to anything described in this blog post so the analysis doesn’t change.

items.headline: Defect Anomalies at a Distance
items.summary: Surface defects carry Weyl and gravitational anomalies that generalize the central charges of two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) and characterize the anomalous response of gapless surface modes to background geometry. These anomalies usually appear as contact terms on the defect. We explain how they are encoded at a distance, in scheme-independent integrated bulk stress-tensor correlators.

items.headline: Room-Temperature Quantum Emission from Boron Nitride Nanotubes
items.summary: Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity.

detail.problem_context: Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information.
detail.method_architecture: As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. detail.findings_tradeoffs: However, dimensionality can be reduced through the implementation of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs). Here we investigate the potential of BNNTs as room-temperature SPEs using confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry. Quantum emitters were found in BNNTs spanning the entirety of the visible spectrum, including spectral regions where SPEs within hBN have not been reported. Furthermore, each tube was found to possess multiple SPEs at varying emission wavelengths along the length, exhibiting lifetimes as fast as 0.5 ns, which is about two-fold faster than the fastest hBN SPEs. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface passivation/coating mitigates blinking events, therefore increasing the emitter stability. Thus, BNNTs can function as a single structure supporting a variety of multiwavelength SPE sources, while maintaining a compact radius of ~25 nm, making them ideally suited for deterministic placement and integration within nanophotonic devices such as waveguides and interferometric filters.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity. However, dimensionality can be reduced through the implementation of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs). Here we investigate the potential of BNNTs as room-temperature SPEs using confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry. Quantum emitters were found in BNNTs spanning the entirety of the visible spectrum, including spectral regions where SPEs within hBN have not been reported. Furthermore, each tube was found to possess multiple SPEs at varying emission wavelengths along the length, exhibiting lifetimes as fast as 0.5 ns, which is about two-fold faster than the fastest hBN SPEs. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface passivation/coating mitigates blinking events, therefore increasing the emitter stability. Thus, BNNTs can function as a single structure supporting a variety of multiwavelength SPE sources, while maintaining a compact radius of ~25 nm, making them ideally suited for deterministic placement and integration within nanophotonic devices such as waveguides and interferometric filters.

detail.problem_context: Compact gauge fields are powerful tools for controlling quantum dynamics and topological phases of matter.
detail.method_architecture: Non-compact gauge fields are particularly relevant for open systems, where particles or energy are exchanged with the environment. Here, we investigate the wavepacket and entanglement dynamics induced by an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: The wavepacket undergoes non-Abelian non-compact Bloch oscillations, in which the spectrum of an auxiliary one-dimensional quantum problem determines the transition between stable oscillations and unstable amplification. In the unstable adiabatic regime, the wavepacket probes an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ topological defect, and its amplification is determined solely by a hyperbolic solid angle in Minkowski space. Threading an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field through a bosonic tight-binding model yields the bosonic Kitaev model, whose volume or super-volume entanglement scaling is governed by the stability of the gauge field. We further propose an experimental realization of an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field in a spinor condensate. Our results can be generalized to other non-compact groups and higher dimensions, providing a geometric framework for entanglement control, selective amplification, and engineering energy transfer.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Compact gauge fields are powerful tools for controlling quantum dynamics and topological phases of matter. Non-compact gauge fields are particularly relevant for open systems, where particles or energy are exchanged with the environment. Here, we investigate the wavepacket and entanglement dynamics induced by an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field. The wavepacket undergoes non-Abelian non-compact Bloch oscillations, in which the spectrum of an auxiliary one-dimensional quantum problem determines the transition between stable oscillations and unstable amplification. In the unstable adiabatic regime, the wavepacket probes an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ topological defect, and its amplification is determined solely by a hyperbolic solid angle in Minkowski space. Threading an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field through a bosonic tight-binding model yields the bosonic Kitaev model, whose volume or super-volume entanglement scaling is governed by the stability of the gauge field. We further propose an experimental realization of an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field in a spinor condensate. Our results can be generalized to other non-compact groups and higher dimensions, providing a geometric framework for entanglement control, selective amplification, and engineering energy transfer.

items.headline: Polynomial-time classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss
items.summary: Sampling experiments are a leading approach to demonstrating quantum computational advantage, yet their robustness to experimental noise is not completely understood. We develop a common framework for classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss, including pure loss. For Fock-state boson sampling, Gaussian boson sampling with fixed uniform squeezing, and fermion sampling with magic inputs, we obtain polynomial-time sampling at inverse-polynomial total variation error, for any fixed nonzero overall loss rate, and with high probability over Haar-random interferometers.

We develop a common framework for classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss, including pure loss. For Fock-state boson sampling, Gaussian boson sampling with fixed uniform squeezing, and fermion sampling with magic inputs, we obtain polynomial-time sampling at inverse-polynomial total variation error, for any fixed nonzero overall loss rate, and with high probability over Haar-random interferometers. A milder flatness assumption on the ideal output distribution suffices for quasipolynomial-time simulation without Haar randomness. With constant thermal loss per layer, the same flatness assumption gives polynomial-time simulation at logarithmic depth. Our bounds for Fock-state boson sampling cover both dilute and saturated regimes and become stronger near full input filling: when only a bounded number of input modes are empty, the noisy output for Haar-random interferometers converges, as the number of modes grows, to a distribution independent of the interferometer.

items.headline: Testing Gravitationally-Induced-Entanglement with Massive Particles and Quantum Clocks
items.summary: We present an experimental proposal to test whether gravity can entangle a levitated particle with an array of quantum clocks. By harnessing the collective interaction between a micrometer-scale particle and an array of ultra-precise nuclear clocks, our scheme offers a conceivable path to observing gravitationally mediated entanglement with quantum clocks in the laboratory. Crucially, this setup will probe a genuinely relativistic effect one that requires the contribution of internal clock energy to active gravitational mass and cannot arise from the Newtonian interaction between fixed masses.
items.headline_tr: Kütleçekimsel Kaynaklı Dolaşmanın Büyük Parçacıklar ve Kuantum Saatlerle Test Edilmesi

Mikrometre ölçeğindeki bir parçacık ile bir dizi ultra hassas nükleer saat arasındaki kolektif etkileşimden yararlanan planımız, kuantum saatlerle yerçekimsel aracılı dolaşıklığın gözlemlenmesi için makul bir yol sunuyor.

detail.abstract_excerpt: We present an experimental proposal to test whether gravity can entangle a levitated particle with an array of quantum clocks. By harnessing the collective interaction between a micrometer-scale particle and an array of ultra-precise nuclear clocks, our scheme offers a conceivable path to observing gravitationally mediated entanglement with quantum clocks in the laboratory. Crucially, this setup will probe a genuinely relativistic effect one that requires the contribution of internal clock energy to active gravitational mass and cannot arise from the Newtonian interaction between fixed masses. Therefore, observing this entanglement would provide evidence for the quantised nature of active gravitational mass -- which has not been tested in any prior experiment -- rather than for spatial coherence of fixed masses,which is routinely tested in matterwave interferometers

items.headline: Beyond Quantum Messages: Toward Quantum-Native Network Functioning
items.summary: The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications. This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities.

items.summary_tr: Kuantum İnternet, genellikle kuantum durumlarını taşıyan ve dağıtılmış kuantum uygulamalarını destekleyen temel kaynak olarak dolaşıklığı dağıtan bir ağ olarak tasavvur edilir. detail.problem_context: The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications.
detail.method_architecture: This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: We first establish the architectural baseline by introducing entanglement as a stateful network resource whose operational condition is non-locally distributed across remote nodes, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades over time through decoherence. Its evolving state must therefore remain visible to the functionalities acting on it. We then move beyond resource visibility and use two mechanisms as proof points of a broader quantum-native functional design space: entanglement generation during propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that can depart from the physical graph. These examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement, rather than by physical connectivity alone. We identify Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction capable of representing such relations while complementing, rather than replacing, classical addressing and signaling. The resulting perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.

detail.abstract_excerpt: The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications. This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities. We first establish the architectural baseline by introducing entanglement as a stateful network resource whose operational condition is non-locally distributed across remote nodes, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades over time through decoherence. Its evolving state must therefore remain visible to the functionalities acting on it. We then move beyond resource visibility and use two mechanisms as proof points of a broader quantum-native functional design space: entanglement generation during propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that can depart from the physical graph. These examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement, rather than by physical connectivity alone. We identify Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction capable of representing such relations while complementing, rather than replacing, classical addressing and signaling. The resulting perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.

items.headline: Spin supersolid in triangular lattice easy-axis spin-1/2 antiferromagnet: a fermionic parton perspective
items.summary: We study the supersolid order of the spin-1/2 easy-axis XXZ antiferromagnet on the triangular lattice using a fermionic parton mean-field theory built on the $π$-flux Dirac spin liquid, with the mean-field order generated by an on-site spinon interaction term and nearest-neighbor (anisotropic) spin couplings. The collective modes are obtained using the random-phase approximation (RPA). In a finite parameter region, we find the Y state as a self-consistent solution, together with the competing Y' state, which is a $90^\circ$-rotated Y state inside the order plane.

detail.problem_context: We study the supersolid order of the spin-1/2 easy-axis XXZ antiferromagnet on the triangular lattice using a fermionic parton mean-field theory built on the $π$-flux Dirac spin liquid, with the mean-field order generated by an on-site spinon interaction term and nearest-neighbor (anisotropic) spin couplings.
detail.method_architecture: The collective modes are obtained using the random-phase approximation (RPA). In a finite parameter region, we find the Y state as a self-consistent solution, together with the competing Y' state, which is a $90^\circ$-rotated Y state inside the order plane.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: The mean-field energy favors Y', even though the two states are exactly degenerate in the classical limit. However, the Y state can become lower in energy when higher-order corrections due to the fluctuations of the collective modes are considered. The Y state can also be stabilized on the mean-field level by applying small external fields, which we do in two different ways: moment-aligned local field and uniform field along the easy axis. In both cases, the RPA calculation for the stabilized Y state gives a roton minimum at the $M$ point in the excitation spectrum. A gapped pseudo-Goldstone mode above the gapless Goldstone mode is obtained as well, which has also been observed experimentally. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of tuning the spinon interaction strength and the anisotropy in spin couplings in our phenomenological model. Comparison with the recent numerical and experimental results is also discussed.
detail.problem_context_tr: Ortalama alan sırası ile $π$-akış Dirac spin sıvısı üzerine inşa edilmiş fermiyonik parton ortalama alan teorisini kullanarak üçgen kafes üzerindeki 1/2 spin-1/2 kolay eksenli XXZ antiferromıknatısın süper katı düzenini inceliyoruz.
detail.method_architecture_tr: Toplu modlar rastgele faz yaklaşımı (RPA) kullanılarak elde edilir. Sonlu parametreli bir bölgede, Y durumunu, $90^\circ$-r… olan rakip Y' durumuyla birlikte kendi kendine tutarlı bir çözüm olarak buluyoruz.

items.headline: From elementary processes to chaos: a discrete-time two-stage contagion model and its continuous limit
items.summary: Two-stage contagion, in which adoption requires two successive contacts with adopters, combined with population turnover produces bistability and relaxation oscillations in Katriel's differential-equation model, but no chaos. We derive from the elementary reactions of the process, without reference to the differential equations, a discrete-time model in which the population is updated in rounds of length $τ$, as in elections, meetings or turns of a game: each individual makes at most one transition per round, events compete as exponential risks, and adoptions take effect from the next round. The model is a Markov chain whose large-population limit is a map $F_τ$; Katriel's equations are recovered as $τ\to0$.
items.headline_tr: Temel süreçlerden kaosa: ayrık zamanlı, iki aşamalı bir bulaşma modeli ve sürekli limiti
items.summary_tr: Evlat edinmenin, benimseyenlerle iki ardışık teması gerektirdiği iki aşamalı bulaşma, nüfus değişimiyle birleştiğinde Katriel'in diferansiyel denklem modelinde iki durumluluk ve gevşeme salınımları üretir, ancak kaos yaratmaz. Sürecin temel reaksiyonlarından, diferansiyel denklemlere başvurmadan ayrık zamanlı bir model türetiyoruz.

detail.problem_context: Two-stage contagion, in which adoption requires two successive contacts with adopters, combined with population turnover produces bistability and relaxation oscillations in Katriel's differential-equation model, but no chaos.
detail.method_architecture: We derive from the elementary reactions of the process, without reference to the differential equations, a discrete-time model in which the population is updated in rounds of length $τ$, as in elections, meetings or turns of a game: each individual makes at most one transition per round, events compete as exponential risks, and adoptions take effect from the next round. detail.findings_tradeoffs: Taking the probability $p$ of adoption after a single contact as bifurcation parameter, with rates and round length fixed, $F_τ$ goes from extinction through a window of chaos to a stable equilibrium; for $β/γ=46$, $μ/γ=0.002$, $γτ=5.5$ the window is $0.023\le p\le0.056$, bounded by the invasion threshold and by a boundary crisis beyond a subcritical Neimark--Sacker point. One-stage contagion ($p=1$), $p=0$ and permanent adoption showed no chaos. The chaotic attractor is essentially unique, with one positive Lyapunov exponent and an outbreak--recharge geometry. In the same window Katriel's equations have a periodic relaxation cycle with troughs of $10^{-44}$--$10^{-164}$: the round structure does not create the oscillation but turns it into chaos and shrinks the oscillatory range in $p$ from $(0.022,0.41)$ to $(0.022,0.056)$. The chaos is therefore not an artefact of discretising a stable state, but a property of two-stage contagion with synchronous updating.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: This may cause systems that act on such data, such as flight controllers and industrial processes, to behave incorrectly or unsafely. Existing defences, such as trusted execution environments and trusted I/O paths, still depend on trusted driver software and correctly configured access control, which remain fragile in practice. In response, we present SensorGuard-RV, a hardware-first approach that delivers sensor samples into processor registers without trusting intermediate software, buses, or memory. After configuration, a write-once ownership switch hands the sensor to a fixed-function controller that performs hardware-level authenticated encryption on sensor samples under a key inaccessible to software. We develop a new RISC-V instruction then instructs the CPU to decrypt the sample and writes it to a register only after verifying its tag and rejecting replays, including across resets. We implement SensorGuard-RV on the NEORV32 core with an ADXL362 SPI accelerometer on an Artix-7 FPGA. At 100 MHz, a protected sample reaches a register in 5,191 cycles (51.9 $μ$s), of which the two Ascon authenticated encryption engines account for 30. Because fixed-function acquisition removes per-byte software polling, the protected loop sustains 19,015 transactions/s, 5.3% above a software-driven SPI baseline. The added logic (3,155 LUTs and 2,215 registers; 5.0% and 1.7% of the device) is dominated by the Ascon engine and preserves the 100 MHz clock, while estimated power rises from 118 to 368 mW.

items.headline: Zirah: A Post-Quantum True Random Number Generator Hardware Signer With an Avalanche Noise
items.summary: Zirah is a hardware signer built around an STM32F407 microcontroller, and its purpose is to find out, on inexpensive hardware, where a post-quantum signing key is exposed and what actually protects it. The device draws every random bit from a reverse-biased 2N3904 junction in avalanche breakdown, amplified by an LM358 and screened by SP 800-90B health tests, computes ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, hedged) on the STM32 with two-share arithmetic masking of the secret-key multiplications, and adds ECDSA P-256 from an ATECC608 secure element over the same digest, once a person has matched an eight-digit digest prefix on its OLED with the PC and pressed a button. A desktop application and a command-line tool drive the board and verify its output, and because only a 32-byte manifest digest reaches the device, it signs files of any type and size, returning signed copies for PDF, Office Open XML, ZIP, PNG and JPEG files and detached records for every other format.

detail.problem_context: Zirah is a hardware signer built around an STM32F407 microcontroller, and its purpose is to find out, on inexpensive hardware, where a post-quantum signing key is exposed and what actually protects it.
detail.method_architecture: The device draws every random bit from a reverse-biased 2N3904 junction in avalanche breakdown, amplified by an LM358 and screened by SP 800-90B health tests, computes ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, hedged) on the STM32 with two-share arithmetic masking of the secret-key multiplications, and adds ECDSA P-256 from an ATECC608 secure element over the same digest, once a person has matched an eight-digit digest prefix on its OLED with the PC and pressed a button. detail.findings_tradeoffs: NIST's SP 800-90B tool rejected the IID assumption for 1,000,000 raw samples and assessed 6.898 bits of min-entropy per byte on the non-IID track, against the 1 bit the firmware credits, while spectral lines near 116 Hz that hold about 5 % of the variance remain unexplained. At 168 MHz the masked signature took a median of 157 ms over 20 runs and a complete signing operation under 0.8 s, and the signer matched the pq-crystals reference in 1,976 checks natively and on an emulated Cortex-M4. The ATECC608 can neither store the 4,032-byte ML-DSA-65 key nor compute with it, so that key sits in ordinary flash behind readout protection, and on an earlier board, before that protection was enabled, a debugger copied it out and the copy produced a valid ML-DSA-65 signature without the device, although the leakage results come from an instruction-level emulator and nothing here is certified.

items.headline: AI-Native Task-Oriented Semantic Communications over a Relay: Benefits and Vulnerabilities
items.summary: Semantic communication (SemCom) using a relay node is considered, where the relay assists in conveying task-relevant information from a source to a destination, with meaning defined by classification labels. A joint end-to-end design of the source encoder, relay transformation, and destination decoders is developed to optimize both semantic inference accuracy and perceptual reconstruction quality for image data. Relay-assisted schemes are shown to outperform direct transmission, with gains that become more pronounced in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes across different relaying strategies.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Alongside these performance benefits, however, a key security vulnerability introduced by the relay is identified, and a Byzantine attack is formulated in which the relay injects structured, learned perturbations into its transmitted signal. items.headline: SoK: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Integration in Software Development: Approaches, Gaps, and Future Directions
items.summary: Standardised post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is critical for protecting software systems against future quantum threats, but standardised algorithms alone do not provide a pathway for their secure integration into software. This paper presents a Systematisation of Knowledge (SoK) of PQC integration in software development, synthesising existing approaches across implementation, migration, and developer education. We analyse these approaches against NIST PQC standards and PQC migration guidance, software development lifecycle coverage, cybersecurity practices, deployment maturity, and testing and evaluation evidence.

Evaluation evidence also remains concentrated in controlled or early-stage settings, providing stronger evidence of technical feasibility than operational readiness. We identify cross-cutting gaps and research directions for developing lifecycle-oriented, empirically validated approaches that connect technical, developer, and organisational requirements for secure PQC integration.

detail.method_architecture: LLM-driven formulaic alpha mining offers an attractive paradigm by combining interpretable symbolic expressions with iterative generation and refinement guided by quantitative feedback. However, existing generation-centric and tree-based search strategies primarily organize factors through generation lineage, leaving structural and statistical relationships across search branches underutilized.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Consequently, information remains localized along parent--child trajectories, which can confine exploration to redundant regions. Moreover, effective factor discovery must account for multiple distinct objectives that cannot be adequately captured by a single search criterion. We introduce CosmosAlpha, a graph-based LLM factor-mining framework that represents discovered factors as a multi-relational graph encoding generation lineage, expression-structure similarity, and cross-sectional exposure correlation. A Graph Flow mechanism propagates search utilities across the graph, allowing each factor to be assessed using relational evidence from nearby factors rather than in isolation. Pareto-guided selection jointly considers quality, fertility and diversity, explicitly modeling their trade-offs within a multi-objective search framework. Across CSI 300 and CSI 500, CosmosAlpha-Graph achieves the best mean rank over seven predictive and portfolio metrics and outperforms its controlled CosmosAlpha-MCTS counterpart on every reported metric, showing a consistent advantage for relational graph search in LLM-driven factor mining. The source code is available at https://github.com/wzhmtldswz/CosmosAlpha

items.headline: MUSS: A Multi-scale and Sequence-based Model for Single-cell Gene Regulation
items.summary: Modeling gene regulation in single cells requires jointly representing DNA sequence, chromatin accessibility, and gene expression across regulatory scales. Sequence-based models capture DNA-level regulatory grammar but often lack cell-level resolution, whereas many single-cell omics models represent genes and peaks as fixed-vocabulary tokens without their underlying sequence. Here, we present MUSS, a sequence-based multi-scale model for single-cell gene regulation that preserves both DNA-level and cell-level resolution.
items.headline_tr: MUSS: Tek Hücreli Gen Düzenlemesi için Çok Ölçekli ve Dizi Tabanlı Bir Model
items.summary_tr: Tek hücrelerde gen düzenlemesinin modellenmesi, düzenleyici ölçeklerde DNA dizisinin, kromatin erişilebilirliğinin ve gen ifadesinin ortaklaşa temsil edilmesini gerektirir. Dizi bazlı modeller, DNA düzeyinde düzenleyici dilbilgisini yakalar ancak çoğu zaman hücre düzeyinde çözünürlükten yoksundur; oysa birçok tek hücreli omic modeli, genleri ve zirveleri, belirli bir anlam olmadan sabit sözcük belirteçleri olarak temsil eder.

detail.method_architecture: Sequence-based models capture DNA-level regulatory grammar but often lack cell-level resolution, whereas many single-cell omics models represent genes and peaks as fixed-vocabulary tokens without their underlying sequence. Here, we present MUSS, a sequence-based multi-scale model for single-cell gene regulation that preserves both DNA-level and cell-level resolution.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: MUSS derives peak- and gene-level representations from DNA using a frozen pre-trained sequence encoder and integrates them through peak-peak self-attention and distance-biased peak-gene interactions. Peak masked language modeling followed by training on paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq aligns these representations with cell-specific regulatory states. Across gene expression prediction, enhancer-gene linking, motif-guided regulatory prioritization, and zero-shot cell clustering, MUSS achieves strong performance against sequence-based and single-cell omics baselines. It further predicts expression for genes and peaks unseen during task training. These results support sequence-grounded, multi-scale representations for decoding cell-type-specific regulatory programs. Code, datasets, and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Lotfollahi-lab/MUSS_neurips26.

items.headline: LinearRaccess: linear-time approximation of RNA accessibility without base-pair span limits
items.summary: Motivation: RNA accessibility is the probability that every nucleotide in a contiguous interval is simultaneously unpaired; it is widely used to predict binding sites for RNA-binding proteins and other RNA-RNA interactions, often in the form of the opening energy, an equivalent measure on a logarithmic scale. Existing tools restrict the maximum base-pair span, discarding long-range base pairs that matter biologically. Others sample structures, introducing statistical variance, or compute accessibility exactly without a span limit, at cubic time cost.

detail.problem_context: Motivation: RNA accessibility is the probability that every nucleotide in a contiguous interval is simultaneously unpaired; it is widely used to predict binding sites for RNA-binding proteins and other RNA-RNA interactions, often in the form of the opening energy, an equivalent measure on a logarithmic scale.
detail.method_architecture: Existing tools restrict the maximum base-pair span, discarding long-range base pairs that matter biologically. Others sample structures, introducing statistical variance, or compute accessibility exactly without a span limit, at cubic time cost.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: No existing method computes the accessibility of windows longer than one nucleotide deterministically in linear time while preserving long-range base pairs. We present LinearRaccess, which computes accessibility directly in linear time via beam-pruned inside-outside dynamic programming with a difference-array aggregation step, without restricting base-pair span. Results: For a sequence of length N and a fixed beam width b, LinearRaccess runs in O(N) time and O(Nb) memory. Against exact accessibility on 12,872 bpRNA-1m(90) sequences of 100-1,000 nt, its median opening-energy error is below 0.001 kcal/mol (0.14 kcal/mol for 700-1,000 nt), and it distinguishes windows of very small accessibility, including 35-nt windows, below the resolution of sampling-based estimates. LinearRaccess analyzes the full 29,903-nt SARS-CoV-2 genome in 419 seconds. Conclusion: LinearRaccess is the first method to compute the accessibility of windows longer than one nucleotide deterministically (without sampling) in linear time without restricting base-pair span. Availability: https://github.com/TakumiOtagaki/LinearRaccess, archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23598502).

items.headline: Learning Strand-Equivariant Tokenizations of DNA with MirrorDNA. DNA has two strands, and for most regulatory label prediction tasks a sequence and its reverse complement should get same answer.
items.summary: DNA has two strands, and for most regulatory label prediction tasks a sequence and its reverse complement should get same answer. Yet DNA language models are tokenized, trained and tested on one strand at a time. We show that this makes them inconsistent.

items.headline: European LD proxies lose tagging for 43% of GWAS leads in the African panel: a chromosome 22 analysis with SwiftLD, an 826-fold faster, byte-identical vcftools LD
items.summary: SwiftLD is a drop-in replacement for the pairwise linkage disequilibrium (LD) modes of vcftools 0.1.17, --hap-r2 and --geno-r2, which population-genetic pipelines use to compute r2, D and D' between nearby variants. On three regions of 1000 Genomes chromosome 22 with 503 to 2,504 samples it wrote the same output as vcftools, byte for byte, and was 826-fold faster (geometric mean at two threads on an AVX-512 CPU). It was also 7.6-fold faster than PLINK 2, the fastest alternative, from VCF input to LD output on all five regions tested; PLINK 2 writes a different file, although its r2 values agree with vcftools' within 10^-6.

items.headline: Protify: A Benchmarking Platform Revealing Task Dependence and Homology Leakage in Protein Language Model Evaluation
items.summary: Protein Language Models (pLMs) have become essential tools for computational protein analysis, and the rapid proliferation of architectures, training objectives, and pretraining corpora has produced a diverse and expanding model landscape. Evaluation practices, however, remain fragmented: studies use different datasets, preprocessing pipelines, and reporting conventions, so results rarely transfer between publications. Here we introduce Protify, an open-source platform that standardizes pLM benchmarking across zero-shot, supervised, and transferlearning settings through a unified, low-code interface.

detail.method_architecture: Evaluation practices, however, remain fragmented: studies use different datasets, preprocessing pipelines, and reporting conventions, so results rarely transfer between publications. detail.findings_tradeoffs: Protify currently supports 35 pretrained models and 61 curated datasets and it is easy to add custom versions of each. Leveraging Protify's high throughput pipelines, we benchmarked 23 models on ProteinGym, discovering that DPLM3B is currently the top-performing self-supervised encoder. Another large-scale supervised evaluation across 32 diverse tasks, spanning enzyme classification, gene ontology annotation, protein-protein interaction, subcellular localization, and other functional properties, found that no single pLM dominated: 14 different models took the top score on at least one dataset, and the margins between the best and second-best models fell within run-to-run variability. Under a homology-controlled split of the same data, every pooled-embedding probe collapsed to near-zero R2, and only a transformer probe over full residue embeddings recovered appreciable signal (R2 = 0.248). items.headline: RPI-Zero: Zero-shot RNA-Protein Interaction Prediction
items.summary: In vivo protein-RNA interactions are mapped almost exclusively by CLIP-seq, which profiles one protein in one cell type per experiment and needs a specific antibody; only about 10% of the roughly 2,000 human RNA-binding proteins have been assayed, and the Protein Data Bank holds around 5,000 protein-RNA complexes, a quarter of them ribosomes. Sequence-based prediction could extend coverage to unprofiled, newly discovered, or designed molecules, but existing predictors are not built for that case. One family trains a separate model per protein and cannot move beyond proteins with CLIP data; the other scores pairs but targets a single RNA class.
